newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Guns galore in rebel-held Albanian city.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Guns galore in rebel-held Albanian city.

text.p: Before the nightly curfew in this rebel-held Albanian city, the hotel guard steps outside and fires his automatic rifle into the sky.
He is warning aggressors not to fire at the Bologna Hotel, one of the finest in southern Albania.

Light sleepers would not relish a stay at the Bologna. The problem is the regular bursts of automatic gunfire that punctuate the night in Vlore where laws are ignored and the authority of the central government has collapsed.
Vlore illustrates the anarchy that has swept Albania since early February when the failure of pyramid investment schemes in which many had sunk their money triggered widespread unrest.
Situated on the seafront, the Bologna has a breathtaking view of the city, but guests are advised to keep their heads down when passing before the windows.
Earlier this month, two cars filled with gunmen sprayed the Bologna with bullets during a 45-minute battle with hotel security staff.
No one was hurt in the hotel, where some Italian journalists were staying, but the shootings were headline news in Albania and Italy.
Vlore and much of southern Albania is under the control of rebel committees who have rejected the authority of President Sali Barisha, whom they blame for the failure of the investment schemes.
An Italian-led multinational security force arrived in Albania this month to protect humanitarian aid deliveries.
Steady bursts of gunfire rang out as a contigent of Italian marines made a brief inspection of the pier.

A carload of Albanian gunmen drove straight up to the small advance force of about 25 men. Their leader, wearing a bullet-proof vest and carrying a Kalashnikov assault rifle, welcomed them to his home town.
"You are my brothers," he said in Italian. "Welcome. If you need any help, you can ask me."
The Italians, the first troops of the United Nations-sanctioned multinational force to reach the south, did not come under any serious threat during their brief foray into Vlore.
Shooting and two loud explosions were heard in and around the city and the soldiers left before dark.
NEARLY EVERYONE HAS A GUN
Albania's arsenals were looted during the insurrection and nearly everyone in Vlore has a gun, local residents say.
One man underscored his point that Vlore is a dangerous place by casually pulling a grenade out of his coat pocket.
"Look," he grinned.

At the hospital across the city, where 52 violent deaths have been registered since the country slid into near-anarchy, doctors said they had regularly risked their lives while trying to help the wounded.
"I know it is dangerous for them, and I am very glad the doctors are working for us," said 22-year-old Ermir Caushi, who was caught in crossfire five days ago and hit in the stomach and arms.
He lay on a soiled, blood-soaked bed in a crowded ward.
In another ward, 39-year-old Hasan Telati explained that he had been shot in the leg by gunmen who ambushed him and some friends as they patrolled their neighbourhood to protect their property.
"We were carrying guns. We had to defend ourselves," Telati said.

The hospital walls are marked with bullet holes. Staff say relatives of victims open fire to intimidate doctors. "A lot of shooting is between gangs who come here to protect their wounded" added Maksi Qejvani, the 43-year-old duty officer.
